tathā ṣaṭtriṃśadeva syuḥ śaive tattvāni saṃkhyayā || 1-88 ||
iti śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevamiśraviracite tantrasārapaddhatau vastunirdeśamātṛkopapattinirṇayo nāma prathamaḥ paṭalaḥ ||

dūrgāṃ ca durgārtiharāṃ viriñcaṃ lakṣmīṃ ca lakṣmīśamapi prapadye || 1-1 ||
translation: I take refuge in Durgā, who removes the distress of those in difficulty, in Viriñca (Brahmā), and in Lakṣmī, and also in Lakṣmīśa (Viṣṇu).
With great reverence I bow to those who, like risen suns, remove the great delusion of darkness.
Having assessed my capacity as far as it extends, I will compose the Tantrapaddhati.
(I will compose it as) another Śruti — a knowledge to be cognized through the prospering ritual-injunctions, mantras, and their meanings.
— variegated, of many virtues, like Viṣṇu's serpent-couch.
— to be served, desired by those who lust, charming, like a lovely woman.
— a life-restoring knowledge, like the herb Sañjīvinī, (attained) through mantras, images, herbs, and meditations.
— another (knowledge) like the Daṇḍanīti, (comprising) the means of rooting out and destroying (enemies).
— as (is) the body of Mura's foe (Viṣṇu) embraced by Satyabhāmā.
— as (is) a year of Brahmā, (constituted) of the kalpas beginning with Kṛta and Tretā.
— another (knowledge), like a fortress, from which misfortunes are driven far away by yantras.
— as here the course of time is bitter through the onset of the Kali age.
— like Brahmā's (cosmic) ordering, dependent on the sequence of the four ages.
— like the form of Vināyaka, elephant-faced, of human shape.
— the sovereign Power that grants liberation, knowable through (spiritual) conviction by those who know That.
— effecting liberation, knowable through its successive sequences, like the triple Veda.
(These) seed(-syllables are) bound by (their proper) metre, seer, and region; (they come) with meditations and with purposes.
Seed-syllables, seed-mantras, mantras, and the mantras called 'garland' (mālā).
Seed-mantras (are those) below ten syllables; mantras (are those) below twenty.

sanskrit: prāyeṇa bālye bījāni siddhiṃ yacchanti bhūyasīm || 1-20 ||
translation: Generally, in childhood, the seed(-syllables) give abundant success.

sanskrit: vārddhake'pi ca sidhyanti mālāmantrāḥ sadaiva hi || 1-21 ||
translation: And even in old age the garland-mantras always succeed, indeed.
But the property of 'thinking' and 'protecting' (inheres) in the signifier-word of the deity.
For his Power indeed has the form of the mantra, possessing the property of thinking and protecting.
Having understood the unity of the signified and the signifier, even in the guru (…).
Indeed, the Mātṛkā is the script of all mantras and also of all words.
— the Brahman whose essence is free of conceptual construction, which has a body of eternal bliss.
Very subtle, long-enduring, pervasive, omnipresent — that (Brahman is) subtler than an atom.
At the beginning of the first creation, from (his) holding knowledge, will, and effort (…).
Sattva, rajas, and tamas — this (triad) has the luster of white, red, and black.

sanskrit: sā śaktirbindutāmeti binduḥ so'pi tridhā bhavet || 1-29 ||
translation: That Power attains the state of the bindu; that bindu, too, becomes threefold.
From the Unmanifest arose the principle called the Great (Mahat), having three divisions.
(It has three forms:) the Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the other called Bhūtādi.
— granting liberation, supreme, divine, bestowing all accomplishments.

sanskrit: hrasvā brahma samākhyātā dīrghā hyaṅgāni ṣaṇmukha || iti ||
translation: The short (vowels) are declared to be brahma; the long ones, indeed, are the limbs, O Ṣaṇmukha.
It arises from the agitation of the bindu, for the fulfillment of the purpose of the Infinite.
Power, Sound, the Great Illusion, and the Ether — thus (it is) fourfold.

sanskrit: vaikharī madhyamā caiva paśyantī cāpi sūkṣmayā || 1-33 ||
translation: Vaikharī and indeed Madhyamā, and also Paśyantī, together with the subtle (Parā).
The subtle (Parā) — a measure of light, exceedingly fine — (abides) within the Kuṇḍalinī.
Paśyantī, self-luminous, should be (understood as) abiding in the Suṣumnā.
She (Madhyamā) is but an inner utterance; she is undivided, moving upward.
(Vaikharī is) thrust forth from the root of the tongue and the lips, having taken on the formed letters.
Then the sound ha, with its modification, was joined with the repha (r).
Indeed, from its union with that (repha), the seed of the Power becomes the cause of the arising of the phenomenal world.
When the two are uttered in close conjunction, that bīja is declared to have a sound-form.
But the sound ī would be Māyā; the bindu is declared (to be) Īśvara.
The sound ha, having attained manifestation, is meant as the inner utterance.
But the syllables beginning with a and ending with ū — six of them (belong) to it.
And through the distinction of the ī-sound, the six syllables beginning with e, being near, (follow).
Because (they are) limbs of the Power, those (letters) are kalās, having the nature of the digits of the nectar-rayed (moon).
(They) have long vowels, end in visarga, are feminine, and have the form of Soma (the moon).
But here is written at the head (that which comes) first in the arising of the vowels.
Air (has) touch as its quality (derived) from the ether; the sounds beginning with k, called 'touch' (sparśa), came to be.
But the group of four syllables beginning with y is the body of air, fire, earth, and water.
But the rest — the (sounds) beginning with ś — are pervasive, accompanied by Agni and Soma, in contact with the vowels.
The (sounds) beginning with k number twenty-five; likewise those beginning with y and those beginning with ś.
And also the consonants joined with the vowels beginning with a, through their mutual conjunction (…).
That very Power has become twofold: the Tāra (Oṃ) and, likewise, the Vāgbhava (bīja).
For this praṇava, called Tāra, is regarded as having the nature of the sound-Brahman.
But that (bīja), bestowing the world, speech, and prosperity, would be the body of Vāgīśvarī.

sanskrit: śaktibījaṃ tathā tāro vāgbhavaṃ ca tataḥ param || 1-56 ||
translation: The seed of the Power, likewise the Tāra, and the Vāgbhava — and then what is beyond that.
And the utterances that arise from its differentiation, sharing in (different) regions, are of various kinds.
The elements beginning with ether, the subtle elements, and the sense-organs (…).
What need of much talk? — the whole (world) whose essence is word and meaning (is contained here).

sanskrit: asyāṃ tu mātṛkākhyāyāṃ lipitvaṃ likhyate yataḥ || 1-60 ||
translation: But because in this (series) called Mātṛkā the state of being a script is written (laid down)…
Because water is called arṇa owing to its nectar-nature, (hence the letters' being) syllables (arṇa) (is explained).
But the material causes of the Mātṛkā, whose self is the universe, are indeed five.

sanskrit: ṭatavargau tathā pādau pārśvayugmaṃ paphau matau || 1-63 ||
translation: The ṭ-group and the t-group are the two feet, likewise; the pair of sides (are) pa and pha, so regarded.
The (sounds) beginning with y (are) skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.
The sound kṣa, together with wrath, is the (final) flashing-forth; (this is) the body consisting of the whole world.
(Everything) from Brahmā down to a blade of grass is established in the Mātṛkā.
From the a-group (the vowels) arose the sun; from the k-group, too, (arose) the son of the earth (Mars).
From the p-group (arose) Saturn and the moon; from the y-group arose the Lord.
From the differentiation of the Mātṛkā's letters, (the following) are described, indeed, further on here.
Likewise, in that enumeration, the Rudra-Powers have emerged.
And the herbs — fifty; likewise the kalās — thirty-eight.
Thus, indeed, has been shown the arising of the Mātṛkā as declared by the Āgama.
Here are extracted the seed-syllables and the seed-mantras, together with (their accompanying) mantras.

sanskrit: tataḥ paraṃ yathāpāṭhaṃ vijñeyā nipuṇaiḥ sphuṭam || 1-74 ||
translation: Thereafter, (they are) to be clearly understood by the skilled, according to the (received) text.
Here they are written, as is proper, joined with the word 'bhagavat'.
The bindu is (drawn as) a staff (with) a half-moon; the visarga is regarded as (consisting of) two bindus.

sanskrit: viṣakālau makāraḥ syād dhātavo yādayo matāḥ || 1-77 ||
translation: The sound ma would be poison and death; the (sounds) beginning with y are regarded as the (bodily) elements.
The sound kha is called 'lord of the world of the vital breaths'; the sound ha is named Śiva.
And pa, pha, ba, and bha, ma, kṣa — they (undergo) interchange, three and three.
Interchange is not approved in the vowels; likewise, not even in conjunct syllables.
Indeed, they serve as the convention for the recognition of each particular syllable.

sanskrit: yathāsaṅkhyaṃ tathā vidyāt svarāḥ sapta diśo daśa || 1-82 ||
translation: So, in accordance with (their) number, one should know: the vowels are seven, the directions ten.
The Vedas are indeed four; the Rāmas are three; the fires are three.
Uktā and Atyuktā, likewise Madhyā, Pratiṣṭhā, (and) Supratiṣṭhitā.

sanskrit: tṛṣṭup ca jagatī tadvat tato'tijagatī matā || 1-85 ||
translation: And Triṣṭubh and Jagatī likewise; then Atijagatī is (regarded).
And Dhṛti and Atidhṛti, and indeed Kṛti, Prakṛti, and Ākṛti.
The count of these meters is prescribed here in some cases.

sanskrit: tathā ṣaṭtriṃśadeva syuḥ śaive tattvāni saṃkhyayā || 1-88 ||
translation: Likewise, in the Śaiva (doctrine), the principles are, by count, indeed thirty-six.
Or the count here may be by nines — with the syllables (numbered) nine, five, (and) eight.
For the easy comprehension of the matters (at hand) indeed (serves) the attainment of what is desired.
That whole seed called the praṇava, pertaining to the Power, they know (to be) like a banyan seed.

sanskrit: iti śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevamiśraviracite tantrasārapaddhatau vastunirdeśamātṛkopapattinirṇayo nāma prathamaḥ paṭalaḥ ||
translation: Thus (ends) the first chapter, named 'The Statement of the Subject and the Determination of the Origin of the Mātṛkā', in the Tantrasārapaddhati composed by the revered Īśānaśivagurudevamiśra.
Aśvīśa, and Bhārabhūti, Tithīśa, Sthāṇu, (and) Hara.
And Akrūra, Mahāsena — these sixteen are the lords of the vowels.
And Ekarudra, Kūrma and Ekanetra, and Caturānana.
And Ardhanārīśvara, Umākānta, and the two — Aṣaḍi (and) Ḍiṇḍin (names; reading uncertain).
